name: Pokémon Arena
description: You are at a dueling arena. You also possess $$$n$$$ Pokémons. Initially, only the $$$1$$$-st Pokémon is standing in the arena. Each Pokémon has $$$m$$$ attributes. The $$$j$$$-th attribute of the $$$i$$$-th Pokémon is $$$a_{i,j}$$$. Each Pokémon also has a cost to be hired: the $$$i$$$-th Pokémon's cost is $$$c_i$$$. You want to have the $$$n$$$-th Pokémon stand in the arena. To do that, you can perform the following two types of operations any number of times in any order: Choose three integers $$$i$$$, $$$j$$$, $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$, $$$1 \le j \le m$$$, $$$k \gt 0$$$), increase $$$a_{i,j}$$$ by $$$k$$$ permanently. The cost of this operation is $$$k$$$. Choose two integers $$$i$$$, $$$j$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$, $$$1 \le j \le m$$$) and hire the $$$i$$$-th Pokémon to duel with the current Pokémon in the arena based on the $$$j$$$-th attribute. The $$$i$$$-th Pokémon will win if $$$a_{i,j}$$$ is greater than or equal to the $$$j$$$-th attribute of the current Pokémon in the arena (otherwise, it will lose). After the duel, only the winner will stand in the arena. The cost of this operation is $$$c_i$$$. Find the minimum cost you need to pay to have the $$$n$$$-th Pokémon stand in the arena.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^5$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 4 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$1 \le m \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$2 \leq n \cdot m \leq 4 \cdot 10^5$$$). The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$$$ ($$$1 \le c_i \le 10^9$$$). The $$$i$$$-th of the following $$$n$$$ lines contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$a_{i,1}, a_{i,2}, \ldots, a_{i,m}$$$ ($$$1 \le a_{i,j} \le 10^9$$$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n \cdot m$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$4 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output the minimum cost to make the $$$n$$$-th Pokémon stand in the arena.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1936C — Pokémon Arena [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
